title: The 'Wow!' Signal: A 72-Second Mystery That Still Fuels the Search for Aliens
summary: Imagine tuning a giant radio dish to the cosmos and hearing a blast so unusual that you scribble 'Wow!' in the margins. That's exactly what happened on August 15, 1977, when astronomer Jerry Ehman at Ohio State University's Big Ear telescope spotted a 72-second radio burst from the direction of Sagittarius. The signal was so striking that it's become legendary in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). The 'Wow!' signal, as it's now known, remains one of the strongest pieces of evidence that we might not be alone. Despite decades of listening, no similar signal has ever been detected again. This has led to intense debate: Was it a natural cosmic event, a glitch, or a genuine alien transmission? The mystery endures, making it a cornerstone of astrobiology. Since that night, our ability to search for life has exploded. We've discovered over 6,000 exoplanets—planets orbiting other stars—and landed rovers on Mars that have found potential signs of ancient life. Yet the Wow! signal still stands out as a tantalizing 'what if.' As scientists continue to scan the skies with ever-more-sensitive instruments, the hope remains that one day, we'll hear something like it again. Until then, the Wow! signal is a reminder that the universe is full of surprises, and the question 'Are we alone?' is far from answered.
why_it_matters: The Wow! signal matters because it focuses the search for life and forces us to ask what evidence would truly prove we are not alone. A confirmed signal would reshape science, philosophy, and how humanity sees itself in the universe.

background_read: Jerry Ehman, an astronomer reviewing computer printouts from Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope, noticed an unusually strong narrowband signal near the hydrogen line, a frequency many SETI researchers consider a logical place for alien civilizations to broadcast because hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.

Big Ear was one of several instruments used in long-running sky surveys to map natural radio sources, and the signal appeared to come from Sagittarius, a constellation in the direction of the Milky Way's center.
Although follow-up observations never repeated the 72-second burst, the event became the most famous candidate in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence.

Since the 1970s, SETI has grown from a few small projects into global efforts, while the discovery of thousands of exoplanets has shifted the question from whether there are places to live to why we have not heard anything.
The Big Ear itself no longer exists, but its data still fuels debate because no other signal like it has ever been confirmed.

perspectives.description: They see the Wow! signal as a strong hint that artificial signals can be detected, even if it was a one-off. To them, the burst justifies continuing and expanding radio searches because it shows the method can find strange anomalies worth investigating.

They argue that an unrepeated 72-second burst is more likely a natural event, Earth-based interference, or an instrument glitch than proof of aliens. Without a second detection or independent confirmation, they warn against treating the signal as solid evidence.

They treat the Wow! signal as a case study in how rare and difficult signal verification is. The growth of exoplanet research and Mars exploration offers more repeatable evidence for life, but the signal highlights the gap between finding a candidate and explaining it.

They focus on newer, more sensitive telescopes and all-sky monitoring to catch a repeat event or similar signal. The unresolved mystery pushes the design of future SETI projects, because catching another Wow! would require continuous, long-term observation.
